extracted.intended_audience: machine_learning researchers and evaluators of large language model capabilities
extracted.subtask_description: Methodology and evaluation protocol for measuring language-model performance on many standardized exams and benchmarks (multiple-choice, free-response, multimodal, multilingual), including contamination checks, prompting, scoring conversions, and simulation procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sourcing of exam materials
rubrics_metrics.description: We sourced either the most recent publicly-available official past exams, or practice exams in published third-party 2022-2023 study material which we purchased. We cross-checked these materials against the model’s training data to determine the extent to which the training data was not contaminated with any exam questions, which we also report in this paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer official public past exams or purchased published practice exams; cross-check against training data and report contamination; note collaborators ran certain exams (e.g., Uniform Bar Exam via CaseText and Stanford CodeX).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple-choice prompting strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: For each multiple-choice section, we used a few-shot prompt with gold standard explanations and answers for a similar exam format. For each question, we sampled an explanation (at temperature 0.3) to extract a multiple-choice answer letter(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run nonholdout/holdout pairs (iterate on nonholdout, then run each holdout once for a final score). In many runs extract the model's letter choice directly from the explanation; in some runs (listed) sample a letter choice at temperature 0 using the already-sampled explanation. Document and fix prompt/implementation bugs (e.g., AMC 10/12 response length bug) and re-run as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free-response prompting strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: For each free-response section, we gave the model the free-response question's prompt as a simple instruction-following-style request, and we sampled a response using temperature 0.6.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use up-to-date public prompts when available (e.g., AP 2022 prompts). For SAT essay use multiple sample prompts and average scores. For GRE use issue and argument prompts from prep materials. Due to human grading cost, do not iterate temperature/prompt extensively; run each free-response question only once at chosen temperature/prompt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Few-shot exemplar usage for free-response
rubrics_metrics.description: We sampled these responses using a few-shot prompt containing one high-quality sample GRE essay response in order to encourage the model to produce appropriately sophisticated text, rather than an unnaturally terse reply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include high-quality exemplar(s) to encourage style/complexity appropriate for human-graded essay tasks; pick exemplars consistent with the target exam's expected level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human grading procedures for essays
rubrics_metrics.description: All free-response questions consisting of formal essays ... were graded by 1-2 qualified third-party contractors with relevant work experience grading those essays. We graded all other free-response questions on their technical content, according to the guidelines from the publicly-available official rubrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use qualified graders with relevant experience; follow official public rubrics for technical content grading; document number of graders per item (1-2) and qualifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling missing images for text-only models
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating text models on multiple-choice questions, we included a text tag stating IMAGE: with a non-meaningful filename wherever an image would be missing. This allows us to lower-bound the text-based models’ performance on multiple-choice exams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly mark missing images so text-only models know an image existed; treat this as a conservative lower-bound on multimodal-capable performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embedding or transcribing images for multimodal and free-response runs
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating multimodal models on multiple-choice questions, we embedded the images into the prompt. For all free-response questions, plus the USABO 2020 Semifinal, we instead transcribed any images and diagrams as objectively as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed images directly for vision-capable runs; for free-response transcribe visuals into text to reduce manual grading load and to make prompts identical across vision/no-vision conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring conversions and percentile computation
rubrics_metrics.description: We synthesized multiple-choice section scores and free-response section scores into overall scores using the best available approximations of the real methodologies: for the SAT, we converted multiple-choice scores into scaled scores using the score calculation chart from an official sample SAT; for the GRE, we converted multiple-choice scores to the 130-170 scale using the official formula of multiplying accuracy by 40 and adding 130; for the AP exams, we used the score calculators found on a public study site, which are based on the point values from the official AP scoring guidelines from 2019-2020. Percentiles are based on the most recently available score distributions for test-takers of each exam type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use official sample charts/formulae when available; when distributions are missing (e.g., AMC 10/12 2022), combine published distributions and report percentile ranges (min lower percentile, max upper percentile). Document assumptions and sources for conversion formulas and percentile references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Codeforces/ELO simulation methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine the Codeforces rating (ELO), we evaluated each model on 10 recent contests. Each contest had roughly 6 problems, and the model was given 10 attempts per problem. After each contest, we repeatedly perform ELO adjustments based on the model’s performance until the ELO rating converges to an equilibrium rating (this simulates repeatedly attempting the contest with the same model performance). We simulated each of the 10 contests 100 times, and report the average equilibrium ELO rating across all contests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simulate repeated contest attempts by iterating ELO adjustments to convergence; run multiple independent simulations per contest and average; report artefacts (e.g., many sims with 0 solves produce low average ELOs) to interpret results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model snapshot documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: We ran GPT-4 multiple-choice questions using a model snapshot from March 1, 2023, whereas the free-response questions were run and scored using a non-final model snapshot from February 23, 2023. GPT-3.5’s multiple-choice questions and free-response questions were all run using a standard ChatGPT snapshot. We ran the USABO semifinal exam using an earlier GPT-4 snapshot from December 16, 2022.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly record exact model snapshots used for each evaluation to support reproducibility and interpretation of results; note snapshot differences when comparing evaluations (e.g., RLHF status, dates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting RLHF impact
rubrics_metrics.description: We ran the multiple-choice question portions of our exam benchmark on the GPT-4 base model and the post RLHF GPT-4 model. Averaged across all exams, the base model achieves a score of 73.7% while the RLHF model achieves a score of 74.0%, suggesting that post-training does not substantially alter base model capability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare base vs post-training (RLHF) on the same benchmark suite; caveat that free-response evaluation methodology may advantage instruction-following models, so interpret free-response differences with caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contamination detection via substring match
rubrics_metrics.description: We measure cross-contamination between our evaluation dataset and the pre-training data using substring match. Both evaluation and training data are processed by removing all spaces and symbols, keeping only characters (including numbers). For each evaluation example, we randomly select three substrings of 50 characters (or use the entire example if it’s less than 50 characters). A match is identified if any of the three sampled evaluation substrings is a substring of the processed training example. This yields a list of contaminated examples. We discard these and rerun to get uncontaminated scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use character-level substring matching on multiple random substrings per example; discard matched examples and re-evaluate to estimate uncontaminated performance; document the sampling strategy (# substrings, substring length).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contamination limitations and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Our filtering approach has some limitations. Our substring match can result in false negatives (if there is a small difference between the evaluation and training data) as well as false positives. We only use partial information from the evaluation examples, utilizing just the question, context, or equivalent data while ignoring answer, response, or equivalent data. In some cases, the multiple-choice options are also excluded. These exclusions may lead to an increase in false positives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge false negatives/positives risk; interpret contamination results conservatively; report contamination fractions per exam and assess their impact (we report contamination overall has very little effect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contamination reporting (per-exam)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each of the exams tested, we show the fraction of questions in the exam which are contaminated (i.e. present in the training dataset). We show the final scores and corresponding percentile of human test takers for GPT-4 (with and without vision) on the full test, and if we extrapolate performance from only the uncontaminated subset of the questions on the test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report contamination fraction, contaminated-only and non-contaminated-only performance, and any computed 'degradation' (non-contaminated minus contaminated) to judge contamination effects; present tables with details per exam.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training-data mixing disclosure (GSM-8K & MATH)
rubrics_metrics.description: To improve GPT-4’s ability to do mathematical reasoning, we mixed in data from the training set of MATH and GSM-8K ... The total number of tokens drawn from these math benchmarks was a tiny fraction of the overall GPT-4 training budget. When mixing in data from these math benchmarks, a portion of the training data was held back, so each individual training example may or may not have been seen by GPT-4 during training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose any inclusion of benchmark data in training mix; quantify relative size; perform contamination checks on held-out test sets; recommend interpreting resulting benchmark performance as between few-shot transfer and benchmark-specific tuning when training mix occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multilingual MMLU translation protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: We translated all questions and answers from MMLU using Azure Translate. We used an external model to perform the translation, instead of relying on GPT-4 itself, in case the model had unrepresentative performance for its own translations. We selected a range of languages that cover different geographic regions and scripts ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an external translation service to avoid evaluation bias from model self-translation; preserve 'A-D' choice tokens and 'Answer' token in English for prompt consistency; be aware translations may be imperfect and may preserve English proper nouns which can affect performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shot-count and prompt-length adjustments for multilingual evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: We incorporated the same MMLU prompt as [4] ... The prompts are composed three-shot, with the three examples picked from the development set. We use three-shot evaluation over the regular five-shot because some languages map to much longer token sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust number of exemplars (shots) based on token-length considerations for different languages; prefer fewer shots if tokenization/length would otherwise inflate prompt size and confound comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple-choice classification by token-probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Finally we classify the correct answer by picking the A-D token continuation with the highest probability from the model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For multiple-choice in translated/multilingual settings, preserve choice labels and select the highest-probability continuation token corresponding to the labeled options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling temperature choices and documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: We sampled explanations at temperature 0.3 for multiple-choice explanations and sampled letters at temperature 0 for some runs; for free-response we sampled at temperature 0.6. These methodological differences resulted from code mismatches detected post-evaluation, and we believe their impact on the results to be minimal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document chosen temperatures for different evaluation modes, note any deviations across runs, and explain reasons (e.g., implementation mismatches or desire to encourage diversity vs determinism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of holdout/nonholdout exams for methodology iteration
rubrics_metrics.description: We sourced each multiple-choice section as a pair of exams: one holdout and one nonholdout. We iterated on our methodology using the nonholdout exam, and then ran each holdout exam once for a final score. We did not source a nonholdout exam for the USABO and for the MKSAP questions and instead ran these once using our best-guess methodology as determined by iterating on the AP Biology exam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use held-out exams for final evaluation only after iterating and tuning methodology on separate nonholdout materials; when no nonholdout is available, document that method and the source of 'best-guess' decisions.
